newsitem.title: USA: Century's worst flooding forces rescues, evacuations.
newsitem.headline: Century's worst flooding forces rescues, evacuations.

text.p: The raging Red River Tuesday rose toward its highest level this century as rescuers saved several people trapped by the floodwaters.
In one such rescue, a Coast Guard helicopter late Monday plucked a family of six from their home near Hillsboro, North Dakota.
"We have had several sorties ... and are getting requests for helicopter and boat rescues," said Bill Stouder, a Transportation Department spokesman in Bismark.
Officials said the Red River, filled with the runoff from melted snow and ice, should reach 38 feet in Fargo before it receeds, which would be the highest level this century.

Residents evacuated the south side of Breckenridge, Minnesota, south of Fargo, after the Boise De Sioux River burst through a dike Monday night. Weary volunteers in Fargo filled 25,000 sandbags into the pre-dawn hours to reinforce makeshift dikes as the river rose about half an inch an hour.

"You really have to search to find any positive news today," said Dennis Walaker, Fargo's manager of public works. Walaker, frustrated by the river's unrelenting rise, said there would be no relief for Fargo residents until Thursday or Friday, when the water level should start to drop.
"The warming temperatures have basically taken the rest of the snowpack and the ice and turned it into water," he said.

In addition to runoff, water from the Sheyenne River, downstream of Fargo, continued to spill out of its banks and into the Red River. In a few days, water released from Lake Traverse will also get into the Red.
Lake Traverse, a reservoir on the Minnesota-South Dakota border, was full and and hydrologists said they had to lower the water to prepare for more drainage from the snow melt.

In Breckenridge, a city of 4,000 on the North Dakota-Minnesota border, a dike that protects the city from the Boise De Sioux River, a Red River tributary, burst. "We lost the south side last night. It (the river) spilled into a residential area," Wilkin County Emergency Services Director Jack Thompson said. "We are evacuating it now."
